verses.text: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you.
Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh!
For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh—
though I myself could have such confidence. If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more:
circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;
as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless.
But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ.
More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ
and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith.
I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death,
and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead.
Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me.
Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead,
I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.
All of us who are mature should embrace this point of view. And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well.
Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained.
Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you.
For as I have often told you before, and now say again even with tears: Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things.
But our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,
who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy (1:1)
context.genre: Letter of friendship and thanks, with an early Christ hymn
context.audience: The church in Philippi, the first church Paul planted in Europe
context.mapLabel: PHILIPPI, PAUL’S CREDENTIALS COUNTED AS LOSS
context.setting: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision and then lists his impressive credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of Benjamin, a Hebrew, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor, blameless in law. He counts all of it as rubbish compared to knowing Christ, and presses on toward the goal.
context.custom: In Philippi, a Roman colony, citizenship was a prized possession. Paul says “our citizenship is in heaven.” The Greek athletic image of straining toward the finish line (v.13-14) also was familiar in Greek cities.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 4 gives final instructions on unity and joy.
context.timelineBible: Paul’s credentials follow the law: circumcision on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), Benjamin (Genesis 35:18), and zeal (Numbers 25:11).
context.sparkNotes: Beware the dogs, the evildoers, the mutilators. Paul had every reason for confidence in the flesh, but whatever was gain, he counts as loss for Christ. He wants to know Christ, the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings. He has not already attained, but presses on toward the goal. Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Savior.

translation.meaning: A coarse word for garbage or dung. Paul chooses it on purpose.
A commonwealth or colony. The believers are a colony of heaven on earth.

otBackground.note: “Whom have I in heaven but you?”

overview.summary: Paul counts his credentials as loss for the sake of knowing Christ. He presses on toward the goal, and says our citizenship is in heaven.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes in prison to the church in Philippi.

history.t: He was a Pharisee, a student of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and a zealous persecutor.
Teachers who insisted Gentile believers must be circumcised.

customs.t: A newborn Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day.
Paul pictures a runner straining toward the finish (3:13-14). Greek games gave a wreath to the winner, as at the nearby Isthmian Games.

archaeology.t: Paul’s hometown, an important city in Cilicia.
The theater goes back to the Macedonian city and was reworked in Roman times. It sits below the acropolis.

overview.discussion: Paul considers his achievements “rubbish” compared to knowing Christ. What do I count on for security that might need to be put in second place?
overview.book: The letter to the Philippians · 4 chapters. Paul’s warm thank-you note, full of joy despite prison.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). In Philippians 3:13-14 Paul pictures himself as a runner who forgets what is behind and strains toward the prize.

currentImage.caption: The ancient theater of Philippi, cut into the hillside below the acropolis. It goes back to the Macedonian city and was reworked in Roman times, so it shows both layers of the colony Paul's readers lived in.
